title: A complete characterization of testable hypotheses
summary: We revisit a fundamental question in hypothesis testing: given two sets of probability measures $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$, when does a nontrivial (i.e.\ strictly unbiased) test for $\mathcal{P}$ against $\mathcal{Q}$ exist? Le~Cam showed that, when $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ have a common dominating measure, a test that has power exceeding its level by more than $\varepsilon$ exists if and only if the convex hulls of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{Q}$ are separated in total-variation distance by more than $\varepsilon$. The requirement of a dominating measure is frequently violated…
